title: Habitats: why the lotus lives in the pond and the cactus in the sand
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers Cambridge Stage 2 Biology, Unit 1.1 'Habitats', Unit 1.2 'Plants in different habitats' and Unit 1.3 'Animals in different habitats'. No textbook needed.
summary: Last year your child found that every place near home is somebody's home. Now they learn the word habitat properly and travel, in imagination and with their hands, to ponds, deserts, forests, seashores and snowy mountains. They find out how the bodies of plants and animals fit their habitats (a cactus's water-storing stem, a lotus leaf that water runs off, a fish's gills, a camel's feet), build a sealed bottle garden that makes its own rain, hunt for animal signs, and argue about whether a zoo can ever be a real habitat.
builds_on: Class 1: every place is somebody's home; living things live where they find food, water and shelter; woodlice choose dark, damp places. Next: Class 3 looks at how plants and animals share one place and help each other; Class 4 studies India's deserts, mountains, plains and coasts and how people live there; Class 5 learns the word adaptation fully, endemic species, and predators and prey.
goals: By the end your child can say what a habitat is and name five different habitats.
By the end your child can explain how a cactus, a lotus and a pine tree are each suited to where they grow.
By the end your child can explain how a fish, a camel and a polar bear are each suited to where they live.
By the end your child can find and read signs that an animal lives nearby (tracks, droppings, nests, holes, chewed leaves).
By the end your child can describe how a sealed bottle garden keeps its own water going round.
By the end your child can give one reason for and one against keeping wild animals in zoos.
words: habitat
the natural home of a plant or animal, which gives it food, water, shelter, space and the right temperature
microhabitat
a very small habitat inside a bigger one, like the underside of a leaf or the inside of a log
suited
having a body that fits its home well (scientists say adapted)
desert
a place that gets very little rain; it can be hot or cold
pond
a small area of still water
gills
the parts of a fish that take oxygen out of water
waxy
covered with a smooth, shiny coat that water runs off
spines
the sharp points on a cactus; they are its leaves, changed
evidence
something you can see or find that shows something is true
condensation
water in the air turning back into drops on a cool surface
subconcepts: a habitat gives food, water, shelter, space and the right temperature
comparing habitats: pond, forest, desert, seashore, grassland, snowy mountain
plants in dry places: cactus stems store water, spines are leaves
plants in wet places: floating lotus and waxy leaves
plants in cold places: pine needles and sloping branches
animals in water: gills, fins and webbed feet
animals in deserts and snow: camel, polar bear, snow leopard
suited to its home: the beginning of the idea of adaptation
animal signs: tracks, droppings, nests, holes and nibbles
a sealed bottle garden: water going round and round
people change habitats, for harm and for care
plants change with height up a mountain

days.title: Every home is a habitat
days.goal: Recall last year's homes and learn what a habitat must give.

steps.title: Remember the woodlice?
steps.do: Ask: 'Last year we lifted a stone. Who lived underneath? Why did they like it there?' (Woodlice, worms, ants; dark, damp, safe, rotting leaves to eat.) Say: 'Scientists have a special word for a living thing's natural home. It is habitat.' Say it together, clapping the three beats: ha-bi-tat.

steps.title: Five things a habitat gives
steps.do: Hold up one hand and name one thing per finger: food, water, shelter, space, the right temperature. For each, ask your child to think of an animal that would be in trouble without it: a fish with no water, a tiger with no space to hunt, a polar bear in Chennai heat. Then ask: 'Is our home a habitat? Which of the five does it give us?'

steps.title: Habitat sort
steps.do: Do Activity a1. Draw six big circles on paper and label them: pond, forest, desert, seashore, grassland, snowy mountain. Your child draws or cuts out pictures (old magazines, or quick drawings) and places each living thing in its habitat: frog and lotus (pond), tiger and hornbill (forest), camel and cactus (desert), crab and coconut palm (seashore), blackbuck and grass (grassland), snow leopard and pine (snowy mountain). For each one ask: 'What does this habitat give it?' Some can go in two places; let them argue it.

steps.title: A habitat inside a habitat
steps.do: Pick up a fallen log or a big leaf (or think of one). Say: 'A forest is a big habitat. But the underside of one leaf is a tiny habitat too, for an aphid or a spider. A tiny habitat inside a big one is called a microhabitat.' Ask: 'Can you find a microhabitat in this room?' (a crack in the wall, the soil in a pot, the corner of the window).

steps.title: Say it back
steps.do: Your child finishes: 'A habitat is…' (the natural home of a living thing, which gives it food, water, shelter, space and the right temperature).

days.title: A habitat in a bottle
days.goal: Build a sealed bottle garden and hear how glass boxes once carried habitats across the sea.

steps.title: Build the bottle garden
steps.do: Do Experiment e1. Build the sealed bottle garden together. Your child chooses where to put each plant, waters it lightly and you close it. Ask them to predict: 'If we never open it and never water it again, will the plants live or die? Why?' Write down the answer and put the bottle in bright light but not direct sun.

steps.title: Story: The Glass Garden
steps.do: Read the story 'The Glass Garden' aloud. Don't explain it. Ask the story questions. Linger on the question: 'Why did the seedlings in the glass boxes live, when the ones in baskets died?'

steps.title: Dr Ward's accident
steps.do: Tell your child about voice v1: a London doctor, Nathaniel Ward, couldn't grow ferns in his smoky garden. One day he found a tiny fern growing all by itself inside a sealed glass bottle where he had put a moth's cocoon in damp soil. The bottle kept its own clean, damp air. Ask the voice question. Then look at your own bottle: is there any mist on the glass yet?

need: a big clean transparent bottle or jar with a lid
a handful of charcoal pieces if you have them
2–3 small plants that like shade and damp (small ferns, moss, money plant cuttings, small creeping plants)

days.title: Plants in dry places and wet places
days.goal: Find out how a cactus and a lotus each fit their habitat.

steps.title: Check the bottle
steps.do: Look at the bottle garden. Is there mist or drops on the inside of the glass? Where did they come from? (Water from the soil and the leaves went into the air and turned back into drops on the cool glass: condensation.) Tell your child the drops will run back down: the bottle makes its own rain.

steps.title: The leaf that water can't wet
steps.do: Do Experiment e2. Drip water on a lotus or colocasia (arbi) leaf, a cabbage leaf and a sheet of paper. Watch the drops. Your child rolls a drop around the leaf like a marble. Ask: 'Why would a plant that lives in a pond want its leaves to stay dry on top?' (So they don't get soaked and sink, so dirt and germs wash off, and so the tiny holes for breathing stay open to the air.)

steps.title: The cactus and the sponge
steps.do: Wet two equal sponges or folded cloths. Wrap one in cling film (or a plastic bag) with just one small hole; leave the other open. Put both in the sun. Ask: 'Which will stay wet longer?' Check at the end of the day. Then look at a real cactus or aloe vera (carefully) or a picture: a thick, fat stem full of water, a waxy skin, and spines instead of leaves. Explain: big flat leaves lose water into the air; spines lose almost none, and they stop thirsty animals biting the water-filled stem. Ask: 'Which sponge is like a cactus?'

steps.title: Humboldt climbs a mountain
steps.do: Tell your child about voice v2: over 200 years ago, Alexander von Humboldt and the botanist Aimé Bonpland climbed a huge mountain in South America and wrote down the plants at each height. Near the bottom: hot forest. Higher: grass and shrubs. Near the snow: only tiny tough plants and lichens. Ask: 'Why would different plants live at the top and the bottom of one mountain?' (It gets colder higher up, like going towards the North Pole.) Ask the voice question.

steps.title: Two plants, two homes
steps.do: Ask: 'Could a cactus live in a pond? Could a lotus live in the desert? Why not?' Listen for: the cactus's roots would rot and it has no floating leaves; the lotus would dry up and has no way to store water.

need: a lotus, colocasia (arbi) or nasturtium leaf
a cactus or aloe vera plant, or a picture of one

days.title: Plants in cold places, and plants near us
days.goal: See how cold-country trees fit their habitat, and find where plants can and cannot grow near home.

steps.title: Snow on a roof
steps.do: Hold a flat plate and a cone made of paper side by side. Sprinkle rice or salt ('snow') on both. Ask: 'Which one holds the snow? Which one lets it slide off?' Show a picture of a pine or deodar tree (Shimla, Kashmir, Darjeeling). Its branches slope down like a cone and its leaves are thin needles. Ask: 'Why would that help in snow?' (Heavy snow slides off instead of breaking branches; thin waxy needles lose little water when the ground is frozen.)

steps.title: Where can plants grow?
steps.do: Walk around your building or street with Worksheet ws1, Section A. Find plants in surprising places: in a crack in the pavement, on top of a wall, on a roof, in a drain, on a tree's bark (moss, ferns, peepal seedlings). Also find places with NO plants: under a parked car, on a busy path, in a dark stairwell. At each, ask: 'What is missing here: light, water, soil, or peace from feet?' Your child records a few in the worksheet.

steps.title: Core worksheet
steps.do: Finish Worksheet ws1, Sections B and C. Read the questions aloud. For the 'why' questions, your child says the answer and you write it in their words.

steps.title: The peepal on the wall
steps.do: Ask: 'A peepal seedling growing on a wall: how did its seed get up there?' (A bird ate a fig and left the seed in its droppings.) 'Do you think it will grow big? What does it need that the wall can't give?'

need: a handful of rice or salt
a picture of a pine or deodar tree

days.title: Animals made for their homes
days.goal: Notice how animals' bodies fit their habitats, and design one.

steps.title: Check the bottle
steps.do: Look at the bottle garden again. Is it still misty? Are the plants alive? Ask: 'We haven't watered it for three days. Where is their water coming from?' (The same water goes round: soil, plant, air, glass, soil.)

steps.title: Body parts and habitats
steps.do: Use pictures or a phone. Go through five animals. For each, point at one body part and ask: 'How does this help it in its habitat?' Fish: gills take oxygen from water; fins and a smooth shape for swimming. Duck: webbed feet like paddles; oily feathers that stay dry. Camel: wide padded feet that don't sink in sand; long eyelashes and closable nostrils against sandstorms; a hump of fat that is food stored for hard times (it is NOT water). Polar bear: thick fur and a layer of fat; white for hiding in snow. Frog: lives in water AND on land, so it has lungs and also breathes through its wet skin. Ask: 'Which of these animals would be in trouble in the others' homes?'

steps.title: Design a creature
steps.do: Do Activity a2. Your child picks one habitat (pond, desert, snowy mountain, seashore or forest) and invents a new animal that would live there well. They draw it and label three body parts with what each one is for. Ask questions: 'Where does it find water? How does it stay warm, or cool? Where does it hide?' A good design gives a reason for every part.

steps.title: Swap the homes
steps.do: Ask: 'Could your creature live in a different habitat? What would go wrong?' Then say the grown-up word: scientists say an animal is adapted to its habitat when its body and ways of living fit it. You'll learn more about this word in later years.

need: pictures of a fish, duck, camel, polar bear and frog (books or phone)

days.title: Hidden homes and animal signs
days.goal: Find evidence of animals we cannot see, and think about zoos.

steps.title: Animal clue hunt
steps.do: Go to a park, garden or field edge. Say: 'Animals often hide. We will be detectives and find evidence that they are here.' Look for: footprints in mud or dust (birds, dogs, cats, cows), holes in the ground (rats, crabs, ants), droppings, feathers, a shed snake skin, spider webs, cocoons, nests in trees, leaves with holes or zigzag tunnels (caterpillars, leaf miners), trails of slime (snails), a broken snail shell near a stone (a bird's 'anvil'). For each clue, your child draws it and guesses who left it. Ask: 'How sure are you? What other clue would make you more sure?'

steps.title: Is a zoo a habitat?
steps.do: Talk about voice v3. Ask first: 'Have you been to a zoo? Did the animals look happy?' Then give the evidence on both sides: zoos have saved some animals from dying out and help people care about wild animals, but many big animals, like elephants, live much shorter lives in zoos than in the wild, and some walk up and down the same path over and over. Ask the voice question. Let your child decide, and give a reason.

steps.title: Best clue
steps.do: Your child picks the best clue of the day and explains to someone in the family who left it and how they know. Check the bottle garden on the way home.

need: a magnifying glass if you have one

days.title: Caring for habitats, and teach it back
days.goal: Think about how people change habitats, play the game and teach it back.

steps.title: Harm and care
steps.do: Ask: 'What happens to a pond's habitat if someone fills it with plastic? If a forest is cut for a road?' Then ask: 'What can people do to make a habitat better?' Good answers: plant trees, leave a corner wild, put out water bowls in summer, clean a pond, keep lights off at night for moths and turtles. Look at your bottle garden: 'What would happen if we left it in hot sun? If we opened it and dropped in a sweet wrapper?'

steps.title: Habitat Hop board game
steps.do: Play the board game g1. When a player lands on a habitat square, they must name one plant or animal that lives there and one body part that helps it.

steps.title: Stretch worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws2 together. Read each item aloud and let your child answer before you write. If your child enjoys it, do Worksheet ws3 another day.

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child shows the bottle garden and the creature design to the family and explains: what a habitat gives, how a cactus and a lotus fit their homes, how a camel or fish fits its home, and how the bottle makes its own rain. Then ask the check questions. Challenge thinkers can try Worksheet ws3.

need: the printed board, a die and counters

sections.p: Write three places you found plants, and one place you found none.
A peepal seedling on top of a wall probably got there because…
Match the plant to its habitat.
A cactus has spines instead of big flat leaves because…
Water runs off a lotus leaf because the leaf is…
The natural home of a plant or animal is called its ____.
Which habitat does each animal live in?
Why can't a fish live on land? Use the word gills.
Why does a camel have wide, flat feet?
A bird with long thin legs and a long sharp beak probably lives…
opts: at the edge of a pond, catching fish
in a hot sandy desert far from water

sections.p: A camel's hump is full of…
A white fox would be best hidden in…
Match the body part to its job.
pairs: saving water and keeping animals off

sections.p: Water drops on the inside of the cool glass are called ____.
Our sealed bottle garden doesn't need watering because…
opts: the same water goes round and round inside
the glass makes water from nothing

sections.p: What would happen to the bottle garden in a dark cupboard? Why?
Who left this clue?
pairs: a leaf with a wiggly tunnel inside
a broken shell beside a stone

sections.p: You find a hole in the ground. How could you find out who lives in it, without digging it up?
Ladakh is very cold and gets very little rain. It is…
opts: not a desert, because it is cold

sections.p: On a tall mountain, as you climb higher you usually find…
Is it a big habitat or a microhabitat?
A frog is suited to…
When an animal's body fits its home well, scientists say it is ____ to its habitat.
Some people say zoos protect animals. Others say a cage is never a habitat. What do you think? Give one reason on each side, then your own view.
The tea seedlings in the story lived because the glass box kept their habitat with them. What would you need to take with you to live on the Moon?
People live in deserts, in snow and by the sea, but they don't have fur or gills. How do people manage?

experiments.title: A habitat in a bottle
experiments.question: Can plants live in a sealed bottle without being watered?
need: a big transparent bottle or jar with a lid (a 5-litre water bottle cut and taped, or a big jar)
2–3 small shade-loving plants: moss, small ferns, money plant cuttings
a spoon and a long stick
steps: Put a layer of pebbles at the bottom (for drainage), then a little charcoal if you have it (it keeps the soil fresh), then a thick layer of damp soil.
Make holes with the stick and plant the plants. Press the soil around them.
Spray or spoon in a little water: damp, not muddy.
Close the lid tightly.
Put it in bright light but not direct sun.
Look at it every day for two weeks. Draw it on day 1, day 3, day 7 and day 14.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'If we never water it again, will the plants live? Why do you think so?'
experiments.observe: Mist and drops form on the inside of the glass, usually in the morning, and run back down. The plants stay green. If it gets too wet and mouldy, open the lid for a day; if it dries out, add a spoon of water.
experiments.why: Water from the soil and the leaves goes into the air as invisible water vapour. When it touches the cooler glass it turns back into drops (condensation) and runs down into the soil, where the roots drink it again. The same water goes round and round, like a tiny version of the rain on Earth. The plants also use the air inside: in light they take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen, and at night they use some oxygen back. The bottle carries a whole small habitat inside it: light from outside, and water, air and soil inside. One bottle garden in England, planted by David Latimer in 1960, was opened only once, in 1972, to add water, and was still growing decades later.
experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts any plastic bottle. Wash hands after handling soil.

experiments.title: The leaf that water can't wet
experiments.question: Why do drops roll off some leaves?
need: a lotus, colocasia (arbi) or nasturtium leaf
a dropper or spoon of water
a pinch of dust or chalk powder
steps: Lay the three things side by side.
Drop a few drops of water on each.
Watch the shape of the drops. Tilt each one slowly.
Sprinkle a little dust on the lotus or colocasia leaf, then drip water and roll a drop across it.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'What will the water do on each one?'
experiments.observe: On the lotus or colocasia leaf the drop sits up like a silver ball and rolls off, picking up the dust as it goes. On paper it soaks in. On cabbage it may sit or spread a little.
experiments.why: The lotus leaf is covered with tiny bumps topped with wax. Water can't spread out on it, so it forms balls that roll off and carry dirt with them. Scientists call this the lotus effect, and engineers copy it to make self-cleaning paints and cloth. For a plant that lives in a pond, it keeps the leaf dry, clean and floating, and keeps its breathing holes, on the top of the leaf, open to the air.

activities.title: Habitat sort
steps: Draw six big circles: pond, forest, desert, seashore, grassland, snowy mountain.
Draw or cut out at least 12 living things.
Place each one in its habitat and say what the habitat gives it.
Put any living thing that fits two habitats on the line between them and explain why.
activities.outcome: A habitat poster with at least 12 living things, each with a reason.

activities.title: Design a creature for a habitat
steps: Choose a habitat: pond, desert, snowy mountain, seashore or forest.
Think: what is hard about living there? (too hot, too cold, no water, waves, hungry hunters)
Invent an animal whose body solves those problems.
Draw it and label three body parts with what each is for.
Give it a name and say what it eats and where it shelters.
activities.outcome: An invented animal with three labelled body parts, each explained by its habitat.

project.title: Our bottle garden diary
steps: Build the sealed bottle garden on Day 2.
Draw it on day 1, day 3, day 7 and day 14.
Each time, note: Is there mist? Are the plants green? Any new leaves? Any mould?
On Day 7, explain to the family how the water goes round inside.
Keep looking for a month and decide: is it a habitat?
project.outcome: A two-week drawn diary of a tiny sealed habitat, and an explanation of how its water goes round.

game.title: Habitat Hop
rules: Put all counters on START. Take turns to roll the die and move.
On a habitat square (POND, DESERT, FOREST, SEASHORE, SNOW, GRASSLAND), name one living thing that lives there and one body part that helps it. Right? Move 1 extra square.
On a trouble square, follow what it says.
On a care square, move forward as it says.
squares: A fish jumps out of the water: back 2
Someone cut the forest for a road: back 3
A polar bear in the hot sun: miss a turn
You left a stone where you found it: forward 1
You put out a water bowl for birds: forward 2

big: Is a zoo a habitat? Is a fish tank? Is a city?
If you could carry a tiny piece of your habitat with you, like the tea seedlings in their glass box, what would you take?
Humans live in deserts, snow and jungles. Are we suited to every habitat, or do we bring our habitat with us?
Who should decide what happens to a pond or a forest: the people who live near it, the government, or the animals who live in it?

challenge.q: Many people think a camel's hump is full of water. Is it?
challenge.hint: No. The hump is mostly fat, stored food for hard times. Camels survive without water for a long time because their bodies lose very little: they make very dry droppings, sweat little, and can let their body temperature rise during the day. Why do you think the 'water hump' story is so popular?

challenge.q: People often say deserts are hot and sandy. Are all deserts hot?
challenge.hint: A desert is a place with very little rain, not a hot place. Ladakh in India, the Gobi in Mongolia and even Antarctica are cold deserts. Antarctica is the biggest desert in the world. What makes a desert hard to live in, then?

perspectives.who: A camel herder of the Raika (Rebari) community in Rajasthan
perspectives.view: Raika families have kept camels in the Thar for many generations and know which desert plants each camel needs and where the hidden water is. Ask: who knows more about the desert habitat, a scientist who visits for a month or a family who has lived there for 500 years? What could each learn from the other?

perspectives.who: A fish in a fish tank
perspectives.view: It has water, food and a little plastic plant. It does not have a river, rain, a muddy bottom, other kinds of fish or space to swim far. Ask: what is missing from its habitat? Does it know?

Winters reach far below freezing and rain is rare, yet barley, apricots and yaks thrive, and houses are built thick, with flat roofs for drying food. Ask: is a cold, dry place a harsh habitat, or just a different one?

voices.idea: Ward was a London doctor who could not grow ferns in his garden because of the city's smoke. Around 1829 he noticed a fern and some grass sprouting in a sealed glass bottle where he had put a moth chrysalis in damp soil. The plants lived inside for years without new water. He designed sealed glass cases ('Wardian cases') and showed that plants could survive long sea voyages inside them.
voices.then: Plant collectors quickly took up the cases. Plants that used to die on ships now arrived alive. The cases were used to move tea from China to India, rubber from South America to Asia, and many other plants around the world, often to make money for empires rather than for the people whose plants they were.
voices.now: His discovery is accepted: a sealed case keeps its own water cycling and its own moist air. The terrariums and bottle gardens people keep today are his invention.
voices.ask: Ward found his discovery by accident, because he noticed something odd in a bottle. What would you need to do to notice an accident like that?

voices.who: Alexander von Humboldt (1769–1859), Germany, and Aimé Bonpland (1773–1858), France
voices.idea: In 1802, travelling in South America, Humboldt and the botanist Bonpland climbed high up the volcano Chimborazo with local guides. They noted that plants change in bands as you go up: hot forest at the bottom, then cooler forests, then grassland, then only mosses and lichens near the snow. Humboldt drew a famous picture showing which plants live at which height, and saw that climbing a mountain is like travelling towards the cold poles.
voices.then: His books made him famous across Europe. Bonpland, who did much of the plant collecting and describing, became much less famous, and the local guides and Indigenous people who knew the mountains were hardly named at all.
voices.now: The idea that plants and animals live in zones set by temperature and rain is accepted. Scientists today are watching many mountain plants creep higher up as the climate warms.
voices.ask: If plants are moving up mountains as the Earth warms, what happens to the plants that already live at the very top?

voices.who: Zoo scientists and their critics today
voices.idea: Supporters say good zoos breed animals that are dying out in the wild and have helped return some, like the Arabian oryx, back to the wild. They say zoos help people, especially children, care about wild animals.
voices.then: Critics point to research such as a 2008 study by Ros Clubb and colleagues, which found that elephants in European zoos lived much shorter lives than elephants in a national park in Kenya or working elephants in Myanmar. Many big, wide-ranging animals pace up and down in enclosures, a sign of stress.
voices.now: Scientists agree that some animals do well in zoos and some do badly, and that big, far-roaming, clever animals like elephants suffer most. Whether zoos should exist, and for which animals, is still argued.
voices.ask: What would you need to see to decide if an animal in a zoo is well? How could you tell, if it cannot speak?

story.title: The Glass Garden
text: The ship rolled, and Ah-Lin rolled with it, and the twelve glass boxes on the deck creaked against their ropes.

He was ten years old that spring, and he had never seen the sea before. At home in the hills of Fujian, the world was green and steep and wet. Every morning a white mist climbed up out of the valleys and wrapped the tea bushes like a shawl. His father and his uncles knew everything about those bushes: when to pick the two leaves and a bud, how long to wither them, how hot the iron pan should be, how to roll the leaves with the heel of the hand until they twisted into dark threads. Ah-Lin was only learning. But he could already smell when tea was ready.

Now his father and uncles had been paid to sail with an Englishman to a country called India, to teach people there how to grow tea and make it. The Englishman's name was on the papers. The tea plants were in the boxes. Ah-Lin had come because his father would not leave him behind.

There were two kinds of boxes on deck. Some were ordinary wooden crates with sacks and baskets of seedlings packed in damp soil. And some were strange: wooden boxes with sloping glass roofs, sealed tight with putty, so that the seedlings inside looked like tiny trees living in a little glass house. The Englishman called them Wardian cases, after the doctor who invented them. The sailors called them coffins.
"They will drown in their own air," said the cook, laughing. "Plants need wind. Plants need watering."
Ah-Lin was given a job: every morning, water the seedlings in the baskets. Do not touch the glass boxes. Do not open them. Not even once.

The first week, the sea was kind. The second week, a hard wind blew from the north, cold and full of salt. It whipped across the deck and spat white spray over everything. Ah-Lin watered the baskets each morning, and each morning the little leaves looked thinner. The wind dried them as fast as he wet them. The salt sat on them in a white crust. By the third week, the seedlings in the baskets were brown and curled like burnt paper. He picked one up and it crumbled.
He sat down beside the glass boxes, very sad, and put his hands on his knees.
Inside the glass, it was misty.

He pressed his face close. The inside of the glass roof was covered in tiny drops of water, as fine as the hairs on a peach. As he watched, two drops joined, and grew heavy, and slid slowly down the slope of the glass, and fell onto the soil beside a seedling's stem.
Rain. It was raining inside the box.

The seedlings in there were green. Not just alive: green, shining, with a new pale leaf unfolding at the top of the tallest one, as soft as a cat's ear. Outside, the salt wind howled. Inside, there was no wind at all. Inside, it was still and damp and warm, and every morning the mist came up off the soil and wrapped the little bushes, and every afternoon it ran back down the glass.
Ah-Lin sat there for a long time, with the cold wind on his back, looking into the box.

It was the hills. That was what it was. Someone had put a small piece of the hills of Fujian into a glass box: the mist, the stillness, the soft wet soil, the water going up and coming down. The plants in the baskets had been taken away from their home. The plants in the glass had brought their home with them.
When his father came up on deck, Ah-Lin took his hand and showed him, without a word. His father looked for a long time too. Then he nodded slowly, the way he nodded when tea was ready.

Weeks later, the ship came up a wide brown river to a city of noise and heat, and then they travelled for many days to the north, up into mountains. The Englishman was disappointed with the first places he was shown. Too hot, said Ah-Lin's father. Too flat. Too dry. Then, one morning, they came to a steep green slope where a white mist was climbing up out of the valley, and Ah-Lin's father stopped, and breathed in, and smiled.
They opened the glass boxes there. The seedlings went into the ground on a cool grey morning, with the mist around their shoulders. They did not seem to notice that they had crossed an ocean.

Many years later, people would drink tea from those hills all over the world, and the papers would say that an Englishman had brought tea to India. Ah-Lin was an old man by then. He knew whose hands had rolled the first leaves. But mostly, when he thought of that journey, he thought of the drop of water sliding down the glass, and the little green leaf, and the moment he understood that a home is not a place. It is everything a place gives you.
story.epiphany: A habitat is not just a spot on a map: it is the conditions a living thing needs (moisture, still air, the right temperature, soil, light). The seedlings in open baskets died because the salt wind took away their habitat; the ones in sealed glass cases lived because the case carried their habitat with them, with water cycling inside (condensation). The turn is Ah-Lin seeing the 'rain' inside the glass. The story is fiction built on real events: in 1851 the plant collector Robert Fortune shipped tea seedlings from China to India in Wardian cases, with Chinese tea workers whose skill made Indian tea possible but who are rarely named.
ask: Why did the seedlings in the baskets die?
What did Ah-Lin see inside the glass box? Where did the 'rain' come from?
What did Ah-Lin mean when he thought the plants had 'brought their home with them'?
Why did his father smile at the misty green slope?
Who do the papers say brought tea to India? Who else should be remembered?

ideas.idea: A habitat is everything a place gives, not just the place.
ideas.more: Water, air, warmth, shelter, food, light and space together. The bottle garden shows that if you can carry those, a habitat can travel.
A cactus's water-storing stem, a lotus's waxy leaf, a fish's gills and a camel's wide feet each solve a problem their habitat sets. Scientists call this being adapted.

ideas.idea: The same water goes round and round.
ideas.more: In the bottle and on the whole Earth, water rises as vapour, turns to drops and falls again. The rain on your window has been through clouds, seas, plants and animals many times.

unknowns: As the Earth warms, plants and animals are moving up mountains and towards the poles. Nobody knows which ones will manage to move in time, and what will happen to those already at the top.
How long can a sealed bottle garden survive? Some have lived more than 50 years, and nobody knows the limit.
Can a zoo ever give a big, wide-roaming animal like an elephant everything its habitat gives? Scientists still argue.

books.title: Over and Under the Pond
books.author: Kate Messner
books.why: A mother and child paddle across a pond while, under the water, fish, beavers and plants live their lives. Shows one habitat and its many microhabitats.

books.title: Over and Under the Snow
books.author: Kate Messner
books.why: Above the snow a girl skis; below it, small animals stay warm in hidden tunnels. A lovely way into cold habitats.

books.title: Desert Giant: The World of the Saguaro Cactus
books.author: Barbara Bash
books.why: The life of one huge cactus and all the animals that depend on it, beautifully drawn.

books.title: Island: A Story of the Galápagos
books.author: Jason Chin
books.why: An island rises from the sea and plants and animals arrive and change to fit it. A first look at how living things become suited to a place.

check.q: What is a habitat? What five things does it give?
check.a: The natural home of a plant or animal. Food, water, shelter, space and the right temperature.

check.q: How is a cactus suited to the desert?
check.a: Its thick stem stores water, its waxy skin and spines (changed leaves) lose very little water, and the spines keep thirsty animals away.

check.q: How is a lotus suited to a pond?
check.a: Its big leaves float and are waxy, so water rolls off; its roots grow in the mud at the bottom.

check.q: Name an animal and one body part that helps it in its habitat.
check.a: For example: fish, gills for breathing underwater; camel, wide feet for sand; polar bear, thick fur and fat for cold; duck, webbed feet for paddling.

check.q: Why doesn't our bottle garden need watering?
check.a: The water goes round inside: from soil and leaves into the air, turning back into drops on the glass (condensation), and back to the soil.

check.q: What is a microhabitat? Give an example.
check.a: A tiny habitat inside a bigger one: under a leaf, inside a log, a crack in a wall.

check.q: Give one reason for and one against zoos.
check.a: For: they breed and protect animals dying out in the wild, and help people care. Against: many big animals, like elephants, live shorter, stressed lives in enclosures.
